Simplify the following powers of \(i\).

  • \(i^{23}=\)
  • \(i^{28}=\)
  • \(i^{41}=\)
  • \(i^{46}=\)

For any positive integer \(n\), we can evaluate \(i^n\) by determining the remainder when \(n\) is divided by 4.

Remainder of \(n/4\) \(i^n\)
0 \(1\)
1 \(i\)
2 \(-1\)
3 \(-i\)

In computer programming, the modulo operator returns the remainder. This operation is used so frequently, that it is often abbreviated to a single symbol (for example, in Python, 5%2 represents the remainder when 5 is divided by 2.)

I will represent the remainders using the Desmos notation.

  • \(\mathrm{mod}(23,4)=3\) so \(i^{23}=-i\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(28,4)=0\) so \(i^{28}=1\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(41,4)=1\) so \(i^{41}=i\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(46,4)=2\) so \(i^{46}=-1\)

To find the remainder using a scientific calculator, I would divide by 4, floor the result, multiply by 4, and subtract that amount from the original.

\[\mathrm{mod}(x,4)~=~x-4\cdot \left\lfloor\frac{x}{4}\right\rfloor\]

The solutions to \(x^{2}-{18}x+{6}=0\) can be expressed, in simplest form, as \(x=h\pm p\sqrt{q}\), where \(p\) might be imaginary. Find the values of \(h\), \(p\), and \(q\).

\(h=\)

\(p=\)

\(q=\)

Write the equation.

\[x^{2}-{18}x+{6}=0\]

Identify the coefficients.

\[a=1\] \[b=-18\] \[c=6\]

Plug numbers into the quadratic formula.

\[x = \frac{-(-18)\pm\sqrt{(-18)^2-4(1)(6)}}{2(1)} \]

Simplify.

\[x = \frac{18 \pm \sqrt{324-(24)}}{2}\]

Simplify.

\[x = \frac{18 \pm \sqrt{300}}{2}\]

Use prime factorization.

\[x = \frac{18 \pm \sqrt{2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot5}}{2}\]

Isolate the twin factors.

\[x = \frac{18 \pm \sqrt{2\cdot2\cdot5\cdot5}\cdot \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

Simplify the square root of the square.

\[x = \frac{18 \pm 2\cdot5\cdot \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

Simplify the integer products.

\[x = \frac{18 \pm 10\cdot \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

Split the fraction.

\[x = \frac{18}{2} \pm \frac{10\cdot \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

Both numerators contain a factor of 2.

\[x = 9 \pm 5\sqrt{3}\]

So, \(h=9\) and \(p=5\) and \(q=3\).

Below is a quadratic function written in factored form.

\[f(x)~=~\left[x-\left(5-2\sqrt{6}\right)\right]\cdot\left[x-\left(5+2\sqrt{6}\right)\right]\]

By finding parameters \(b\) and \(c\), the same function can be expressed in standard form:

\[f(x)~=~x^2+bx+c\]

Find \(b\) and \(c\).

\(b=\)

\(c=\)

Start in factored form.

\[f(x)~=~\left[x-(5-2\sqrt{6})\right]\cdot\left[x-(5+2\sqrt{6})\right]\]

At this point, you can either FOIL or distribute away the inside parentheses. I think it'll be a bit cleaner to distribute the subtraction across the parentheses.

\[\left[x-5+2\sqrt{6}\right]\cdot\left[x-5-2\sqrt{6}\right]\]

But now, instead of FOIL, we need to generalize, because each factor has three terms: a linear term and two constant terms. You could probably guess that we simply multiply each of the first factor's terms by each of the second factor's terms.

\[x^2-5x-2\sqrt{6}x-5x+25+10\sqrt{6}+2\sqrt{6}x-10\sqrt{6}-24\]

Combine like terms. Opposite terms cancel each other out.

\[x^2-10x+1\]

Thus, \(b=-10\) and \(c=1\).

Consider the quadratic equation:

\[{7}x^{2}+{12}x+{6}=0\]

Does the equation have two real solutions, one real solution, or two complex solutions?

Hint: Calculate the discriminant.

The discriminant, \(D\), is the expression under the radical in the quadratic formula.

\[D=b^2-4ac\]

If Then
\(D<0\) There are two complex solutions
\(D=0\) There is one real solution
\(D>0\) There are two real solutions

Calculate the discriminant.

\[D=(12)^2-4(7)(6)\]

\[D=144-168\]

\[D=-24\]

Because \(D<0\) we know the equation has two complex solutions.

Consider the quadratic equation:

\[{10}x^{2}+{6}x+1=0\]

Does the equation have two real solutions, one real solution, or two complex solutions?

Hint: Calculate the discriminant.

The discriminant, \(D\), is the expression under the radical in the quadratic formula.

\[D=b^2-4ac\]

If Then
\(D<0\) There are two complex solutions
\(D=0\) There is one real solution
\(D>0\) There are two real solutions

Calculate the discriminant.

\[D=(6)^2-4(10)(1)\]

\[D=36-40\]

\[D=-4\]

Because \(D<0\) we know the equation has two complex solutions.

Define function \(f\) with equation \(f(x)~=~{2}x^{2}+{5}x+{7}\).

Evaluate \(f(-4-3i)\).

\[f(-4-3i) ~=~ 2(-4-3i)^2+5(-4-3i)+7\]

The most challenging part is squaring the complex input. Remember, raising to the power of 2 means multiplying by itself. When we multiply two complex numbers, we basically "FOIL".

\[(-4-3i)^2~\equiv~(-4-3i)(-4-3i)~\equiv~16+12i+12i+9i^2\]

Remember, \(i^2=-1\).

\[(-4-3i)^2~\equiv~16+12i+12i-9\]

Combine like terms.

\[(-4-3i)^2~\equiv~7+24i\]

So, now return to the full expression, replacing \((-4-3i)^2\) with \(7+24i\).

\[f(-4-3i) ~=~ 2(7+24i)+5(-4-3i)+7\]

Distribute.

\[f(-4-3i) ~=~ 14+48i-20-15i+7\]

Combine like terms.

\[f(-4-3i) ~=~ 1+33i\]

So, type your answer as 1+33i.
